title: Why Effort matters
text: Weight and reps tell us what you did. Effort tells us how hard it felt, which helps make the next suggestion more useful.

title: You do not need a perfect Effort score
text: Pick the option that best matches how the set felt. Honest and consistent is more useful than trying to be exact.

title: One good day is useful
text: Repeating a strong session helps show whether the result is something you can rely on.

title: Progress can be repeatability
text: Doing the same hard work with better control or less struggle can be progress too.

title: Expect the reps to feel harder
text: When you add weight, it is normal for the rep count to drop at first.

title: Keep the increase small
text: A small step makes it easier to keep your technique and learn whether the new load is sustainable.

title: Lighter does not mean easier training
text: A small drop can let you get better reps and rebuild momentum.

title: Quality can come before load
text: If the current weight keeps cutting your reps short, lowering it can give you a better training set.

title: Your old best is not today's target
text: After time away, use the first session to learn where you are now.

title: Come back in steps
text: A steady return gives you better information than trying to match an old peak immediately.

title: More reps can be real progress
text: You can improve without adding weight every session.

title: Own the current load first
text: If you can add good reps while keeping the same setup, the load is still giving you room to progress.

title: Your first session is a baseline
text: The goal is to find a load or version you can control, not to test your maximum.

title: A few sessions tell a better story
text: More comparable workouts make it easier to see what is actually changing.

title: Keep the conditions similar
text: Distance, time, surface and load all affect conditioning work. Compare like with like.

title: Your job is to give a good effort
text: You do not need a personal best every workout. A solid session you can recover from is useful.

title: Do not rush the next number
text: Progress that you can repeat is usually more useful than one forced jump.

title: Your log is for you
text: There is no benefit in making a hard set look easy. Honest logging makes future guidance better.

title: Small wins count
text: One cleaner rep, one extra rep, or the same work with better control can all be useful progress.

title: Compare with your own pattern
text: The useful question is whether your training is improving over time, not whether your number matches someone else's.

title: One rough session is not a trend
text: Sleep, stress and normal day-to-day changes can affect a workout. Look at the pattern, not one result.

title: One great session is not a promise
text: A strong day is useful information. Repeating it tells you more.

title: You can adjust the suggestion
text: If a load clearly feels wrong today, change it. The app is guidance, not a command.

title: Simple and repeatable wins
text: A routine you can keep doing is more useful than a perfect plan you cannot follow.

title: Every logged session teaches the app
text: Your history becomes more useful when you keep the exercise, setup and Effort notes consistent.

title: Consistency matters more than fancy methods
text: Regular resistance training is the main driver. Most people do not need complicated techniques to make progress.

title: Heavier loads help strength more
text: Higher loads tend to be better for maximal strength, while muscle growth can happen across a wider range of loads.

title: You do not need failure every set
text: Research does not show that every set must reach complete failure to build strength or muscle.

title: Range changes the exercise
text: Full-range training often works well for strength and lower-body muscle growth. The best range still depends on the exercise and person.

title: There is no magic slow rep speed
text: Muscle growth has been seen across a wide range of normal rep speeds. Very slow reps are not required.

title: Random exercise changes are not automatically better
text: Some planned variety can help, but changing exercises too often can make progress harder to track.

title: Feeling capable helps motivation
text: Exercise research links feeling competent and having more personal choice with better long-term engagement.

title: Frequency is one way to spread your work
text: Training a muscle more often can help spread your weekly work. Frequency is only one part of the plan.

title: Keep the elbow position repeatable
text: If the elbow moves a lot as the set gets hard, the exercise changes. Keep the arm position similar when comparing sessions.

title: Do not force the lockout with your whole body
text: Use a load you can finish without turning the last reps into a body swing or press.

title: Small jumps are enough
text: Triceps exercises often respond well to a few extra clean reps before the next load increase.

title: Keep your setup the same
text: For a custom exercise, use the same setup and range each time so your log stays easy to compare.

title: Change one thing at a time
text: If you change load, try to keep the setup and range the same. That makes progress easier to understand.

title: Use clean reps as your guide
text: If you are not sure how to progress a custom exercise, keep the reps controlled and make small changes.

title: Keep the movement repeatable
text: A custom exercise is easier to track when the range, grip and body position stay similar.

title: Small progress still counts
text: A few more good reps or a small load change can be enough. You do not need a big jump.

title: Let your history build
text: The more consistently you log a custom exercise, the more useful its progress pattern becomes.
